summary: Children learn that knowing one of area or perimeter does NOT determine the other: two shapes can share an area yet have different perimeters, and share a perimeter yet have different areas. (They are not completely unrelated, though: for example, a fixed perimeter limits how large the area can be.) The core work is systematic — fix one quantity (e.g. area 24 cm²) and generate shapes that differ in the other, tabulating so the variation is SEEN, not asserted. The target misconception is the intuitive 'Same A – Same B' rule (same area must mean same perimeter, and vice versa). Because a correct answer can come from the faulty intuition, always probe the reasoning.
misconceptions: 'Same A – Same B': believes shapes with equal area must have equal perimeter (or that changing sides by equal-and-opposite amounts leaves both unchanged).
Conflates area and perimeter, so cannot hold one fixed while varying the other.
Thinks making a shape 'bigger' must increase area and perimeter together.

activities.title: Lock the area, watch the perimeter change
steps: Start from a 4×6 rectangle on squared paper (or a drag-to-reshape grid) that reads 'Area 24 cm², Perimeter 20 cm'.
Reshape it to 3×8, 2×12, then 1×24, keeping the area pinned at 24 cm² each time.
After each shape, count the squares to confirm the area is still 24, then count the edge units to find the new perimeter (20, 22, 28, 50 cm).
Record each rectangle's dimensions and perimeter in a table so the growing perimeter is visible alongside the unchanged area.
Say aloud what stays the same and what changes.
activities.insight: Keeping area fixed while reshaping shows the perimeter climbing even though the covered surface is unchanged, so same area does NOT force same perimeter.

activities.title: Lock the perimeter, watch the area change
steps: Fix a perimeter (e.g. 20 cm) and build several rectangles that all have that perimeter: 1×9, 2×8, 3×7, 4×6, 5×5.
For each, count the squares to find the area (9, 16, 21, 24, 25 cm²) and record it in a table.
Note which shape gives the largest area and which the smallest for the same perimeter.
activities.insight: With perimeter held constant, the area varies — so same perimeter does NOT force same area either; in both directions, fixing one quantity does not fix the other (although the fixed perimeter does cap the area: here the 5×5 square gives the most).

activities.title: The string test (predict, then check)
steps: Look at a 3×4 rectangle and a 2×6 rectangle on squared paper; confirm both have area 12 cm² by counting squares.
PREDICT whether one loop of string will go exactly around both, and say WHY before testing.
Lay the string around each and measure: the 3×4 needs 14 cm, the 2×6 needs 16 cm.
Draw a THIRD rectangle with area 12 but yet another perimeter, and find the largest perimeter you can make for area 12 (with whole-number sides, the thinnest 1×12 gives 26 cm).
activities.insight: Both rectangles cover the same area (12 cm²) but their perimeters differ (14 cm and 16 cm) — a direct counterexample to 'Same A – Same B'.

activities.title: Convince the sceptic
steps: Respond to a character who insists 'same area must mean same perimeter' and 'bigger area always means bigger perimeter'.
Build or draw counterexamples and use them to explain, in your own words, why the character is wrong.
Answer the follow-up: 'If two shapes have the same perimeter, must they have the same area? Show me two that don't.'
activities.insight: Articulating the reason — that area and perimeter vary separately — consolidates understanding beyond producing a correct answer.

checkQuestion: Here are two rectangles: one is 3 cm by 4 cm, the other 2 cm by 6 cm. Do they have the same area? Do they have the same perimeter? Explain your reasoning.
checkAnswer: Both have area 12 cm² (same area), but their perimeters are 14 cm and 16 cm (different) — so the same area can have different perimeters; area and perimeter are independent.
